stops.name: Castellammare di Stabia, born to the Lampetielli
stops.date_confidence: attested; it.wikipedia 'Assunta Maresca' gives 19 January 1935 at Castellammare di Stabia. CONTRADICTION: English Wikipedia counts four brothers, it.wikipedia names only Pasquale and Ciro. English Wikipedia calls the uncle Vincenzo a known Camorra boss; it.wikipedia records only his seven-year sentence for killing his own brother Gerardo. The nickname is 'Lampetielli' in it.wikipedia and 'i Lampatielli' in the English. Pin inherited byte-identically from pasquale_simonetti_pascalone_e_nola.journey.json (40.6952, 14.483); values of 40.6978 and 40.6989 drafted in this pass are not used.
stops.campa: In Castellammare di Stabia, under Vesuvius on the far arm of the bay, Assunta Maresca is born to Alberto Maresca, who moves cigarettes, and into a house the town calls the Lampetielli for the way its men handle a blade. Her uncle Vincenzo has already served seven years for killing his own brother Gerardo. She is the daughter among the sons; her brothers Pasquale and Ciro carry the name into the same trade. The town is a shipyard town and a smuggling town at once. The English record counts four brothers where the Italian names two, and calls the uncle a Camorra boss where the Italian gives only the sentence.

The criminal file of Vincenzo Maresca, convicted of the murder of his brother Gerardo

stops.name: Castellammare di Stabia, the house with no address

stops.campa: The Maresca household works the contraband trade out of this town, and that is the whole of what the record holds. No source names the street, the house, the boats, the landing place, or the goods beyond cigarettes. A family that lives by not being written down is not written down. What survives is a nickname taken from the way the men of the house use a knife, and a sentence passed on an uncle for killing his brother. Nothing more exact than the town centre can be marked.

The episode is recorded on one English-language site and appears in no Italian encyclopedia entry consulted, which is why it stands here as tradition rather than fact. Every later act she is accused of reaches a courtroom, and each of those later cases is documented on both sides of the language divide. This one never does, and the pretura records for the late 1940s are unexamined.

The islet faces Torre Annunziata but belongs to her own town, which is the sort of thing the English sources get wrong and the maps do not.

stops.name: Palma Campania, the carter's son
stops.date_confidence: attested; date and town agree across it.wikipedia 'Pasquale Simonetti' and English Wikipedia. stops.campa: Nine years before her, on the inland plain behind Vesuvius, Pasquale Simonetti is born. He forges ration books through the war and comes out of it holding the fruit and vegetable exchange at Corso Novara, where he sets the price a quintal of potatoes may be sold at and takes his percentage for setting it. Nola gives him the name he is known by: Pascalone 'e Nola. His story begins in this town and follows him to Corso Novara; hers joins it at the wedding of April 1955.
suggested_refs: Civil registers of Palma Campania, February 1926

stops.name: Corso Novara, the president of prices
stops.date_confidence: the year is a placeholder; no source dates his market ascendancy beyond the early 1950s. Pin inherited byte-identically from pasquale_simonetti_pascalone_e_nola.journey.json (40.8557, 14.2712), whose own note records that three drafted values for this street disagreed and all three fell southeast of it.
stops.campa: East of the central station, between the tracks and the wholesale sheds, the fruit and vegetable exchange of Naples decides what Campania eats and what Campania pays. Simonetti holds it jointly with Antonio Esposito of Pomigliano d'Arco, and the partnership will not hold. He is shot on this street, and she kills on it: eighty days after the wedding, and eighty days after that. She has not seen it yet. She is in Castellammare, being photographed. No record of the exchange itself has been examined for these years.

CONTRADICTION on the venue, unresolved: an earlier pass drafted the Pontifical Shrine of Pompei, which no Wikipedia edition supports; Il Mattino places the ceremony in an old church outside Castellammare di Stabia with the banquet on the Pozzano hillside and gives about three hundred guests; the atlas inherits Palma Campania from pasquale_simonetti_pascalone_e_nola.journey.json, which found three sources for the town.
stops.campa: She marries Pasquale Simonetti, already carrying his child. Camorristi come from across the province to eat at the wedding, among them Giuseppe Maisto and Antonio Esposito, the rivals. stops.date_confidence: single source (napolitan.it, reaching the atlas through pasquale_simonetti_pascalone_e_nola.journey.json), uncorroborated. This is NOT the wedding venue; the marriage is placed at Palma Campania. Pin inherited byte-identically at 40.7486, 14.501.
stops.campa: After the ceremony the couple go to the sanctuary at Pompei, and there, one account holds, a pistol is left at the shrine. The detail rests on a single Neapolitan site and on no encyclopedia. It is kept because it is the only object anyone bothered to describe from the whole wedding day, and because the question of weapons returns in October, when investigators count shots from at least four pistols in Corso Novara and no source will say whose hands held them.

stops.date_confidence: 16 July is attested by both English Wikipedia articles, terranostranews.it and italiamistero.it, and is confirmed arithmetically by the eighty days from the wedding; it.wikipedia 'Assunta Maresca' gives 15 July and the dissent is left standing. stops.campa: Eighty days after the wedding Simonetti walks into Corso Novara near the wholesale sheds and meets Gaetano Orlando, sent by Antonio Esposito. One account says a greeting goes unreturned and that this is the signal. He is hit in the stomach in the open street in the morning, and some accounts name Gaetano Nuvoletta as the accomplice. His wife is six months pregnant in Castellammare and learns of it by telephone. The market goes on selling potatoes at the price he set.

stops.date_confidence: CONTRADICTION, unresolved. internapoli.it alone separates the shooting (16 July) from the death by peritonitis (17 July); English Wikipedia and italiamistero.it collapse both into 16 July; it.wikipedia 'Assunta Maresca' gives 15 July. stops.name: Castellammare di Stabia, the widow at twenty
stops.date_confidence: RECONSTRUCTION as to the date; no source records her movements or her intentions between the death and 4 October. The widowhood and the pregnancy at six months are attested by both Wikipedia editions. Pin inherited byte-identically.
stops.campa: She comes back to her father's town a widow at twenty with a child due in the winter. The Lampetielli name means what it has always meant. Nothing in the record describes these eleven weeks: no statement, no threat, no meeting, no witness who saw her decide anything. What the record holds is a departure on 4 October and an arrival in Corso Novara. Between the burial no source describes and the killing everyone saw, the record is empty, and that is the stretch the films fill.

Asked why she held the gun in both hands, she gives the only line anyone remembers from that day.

stops.name: Poggioreale, the arrest
stops.date_confidence: attested; sources give either 13 or 14 October 1955, and it.wikipedia and English Wikipedia agree on the 14th. Pin inherited byte-identically at 40.86, 14.2789; the 40.8524, 14.2961 drafted in this pass falls about 1.7 km east, near the cemetery and Doganella.
stops.campa: Ten days after the killing she is taken and brought to the prison on Via Nuova Poggioreale. She does not deny the act at any point in the sixty-six years that follow. What she disputes, then and to the end, is the word for it: not an execution but a defence, of herself and of the child she is carrying, against a man who would have done to her what he did to her husband. The prosecution will call it premeditation. The word the country uses is honour.

stops.name: Ottaviano, the Fiat 128
stops.date_confidence: attested; Aldo Semerari was killed on 1 April 1982 and his decapitated body found in a Fiat 128 at Ottaviano (it.wikipedia 'Aldo Semerari'). An earlier pass in this research dated the murder to 1981, which is wrong. Coordinates are the town centre of Ottaviano, supplied by the atlas; no source gives the exact spot.
stops.campa: Aldo Semerari, forensic psychiatrist, who wrote expert opinions for Cutolo's men and for their enemies in the same years, is found decapitated in a car at Ottaviano, Cutolo's own town. His head is on the seat beside him. She is charged in connection with the murder. Ammaturo will take responsibility for the beheading twenty-eight years later, in an interview, saying the man was a traitor; the judges who heard his account did not believe it and acquitted the men he named as executants.
suggested_refs: The Semerari homicide file, Ottaviano, April 1982, unexamined

stops.name: Naples, the apartment and the second arrest
stops.date_confidence: attested that the arrest followed shortly after the 13 February press conference (it.wikipedia 'Umberto Ammaturo'); no exact date is given and 1 May is a placeholder. CONTRADICTION, unresolved: it.wikipedia records acquittal on the Semerari murder, on attempted extortion of a bank and on drug trafficking; English Wikipedia records conviction and four years served, single-sourced. Canonical Naples pin; the address of the apartment is not documented.
stops.campa: Carabinieri find her in a Naples apartment with Ammaturo and arrest them both. The charges are extortion, drug trafficking, and the killing of Semerari. She denies the murder for the remaining thirty-nine years of her life. On the outcome the record splits and does not close: the Italian encyclopedia says she was acquitted on all three counts, the English says she was convicted and served four years. The address of the apartment is not documented. She is forty-seven, and it is the second time the state has taken her.
suggested_refs: Custody and judgment records of the 1982 Naples proceedings, unexamined

stops.name: Naples, the film she stops
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, for the blocking, and for the directors by it.wikipedia. The Alessandra Mussolini casting and the phrase 'affront to her honour' come from English Wikipedia and from Christina Newland's Substack, where the only word inside quotation marks is 'affront'; the phrase is therefore rendered as narration here and not as a quotation. Month and day are defaults. Canonical Naples pin.
stops.campa: RAI has made a television film of her life, Il caso Pupetta Maresca, directed by Marisa Malfatti and Riccardo Tortora. She calls the casting an affront to her honour, goes to court, and the broadcast is blocked. The actress cast as her is Alessandra Mussolini, granddaughter of Benito, a detail the English record carries and the Italian does not. It is the second time a film of her has been released before she could answer it, and the first time she has been able to stop one.
sources: Christina Newland, 'The Little Doll of Naples'
suggested_refs: Il caso Pupetta Maresca (1982), dir. Marisa Malfatti and Riccardo Tortora, RAI

stops.name: Castel Capuano, acquitted of ordering Galli's death
stops.date_confidence: attested by it.wikipedia 'Assunta Maresca' for the 1985 acquittal in the Galli case after a prosecution demand for life; month and day are defaults. The acquittals on the Semerari and bank-extortion and trafficking charges are attested by the same page and are undated there. No source names the courthouse; Castel Capuano is inference, and the pin is inherited byte-identically.
stops.campa: The prosecutor had asked for life. She is acquitted for lack of evidence. On the Semerari charge, and on the attempted extortion of a bank, and on the trafficking, the Italian record gives the same word three more times. The state has now failed to convict her of anything since 1959 and has held her in custody for years in the attempt, which is a distinction the newspapers do not make when they call her the first woman of the Camorra. She is fifty. The one conviction that stands in law against her name is still the 1959 one, which she has never denied.
suggested_refs: The 1985 judgment in the Galli case, court unnamed in the sources

stops.name: Tribunale di Napoli, the assets taken
stops.date_confidence: attested by it.wikipedia 'Assunta Maresca' for the year; month and day are defaults. The quoted interview is undated in interris.it and is placed at this stop for its subject, not on evidence of when it was given. Pin inherited byte-identically at the Castel Capuano value.
stops.campa: The tribunal declares her an affiliate of the Camorra clan Nuova Famiglia and orders her property confiscated. She has been acquitted in the criminal courts; the preventive measure does not require a conviction, and it takes what the trials could not. This is the sentence that ends her working life. She keeps saying, in interviews for the next thirty-five years, that it was the second imprisonment that hurt, and that it was for having talked about Cutolo.
stops.quote: il carcere che mi ha fatto veramente male è stato quando sono stata arrestata la seconda volta, per avere parlato di Cutolo
stops.quote_source: Interview, undated in the source; quoted in interris.it, 'Morta Pupetta Maresca, la prima camorrista'
suggested_refs: The 1986 confiscation order of the Tribunale di Napoli

stops.name: Bellizzi Irpino, the parties in the prison
stops.date_confidence: attested by it.wikipedia 'Assunta Maresca', citing a la Repubblica report of 18 March 1989 on the prison scandal, which supplies the only date anchor for her time at this facility. it.wikipedia states the gatherings as fact ('La donna gestiva feste cui partecipavano magistrati e alte personalita'), not as allegation. Coordinates corrected: Bellizzi Irpino is at 40.8901, 14.7982; the 40.931, 14.7726 drafted in this pass falls about 5 km northwest of Avellino.
stops.campa: In the prison at Bellizzi Irpino outside Avellino she runs gatherings attended by magistrates and other high personalities. la Repubblica reports it in March 1989 as a scandal of the prison rather than as an allegation against her: the story is told against the officials who came, not against the prisoner who invited them. That report of 18 March 1989 is the only date anchor for her time in this prison, and the dates of her imprisonment here are given by no source consulted.
suggested_refs: The 1989 inquiry into the Bellizzi Irpino prison, unexamined

stops.name: Naples, Umberto in Peru
stops.date_confidence: attested that Ammaturo was arrested in 1993 and decided to collaborate 'pochi mesi dopo' (it.wikipedia 'Umberto Ammaturo'); the month is not named and the June 1993 date drafted in an earlier pass of this research is unsupported. The explicit Semerari confession is recorded by it.wikipedia 'Aldo Semerari' from a May 2010 interview. The quotation is undated in every source reached; only its occasion is given. Canonical Naples pin.
stops.campa: Ammaturo is arrested in Peru with a new companion, Yohanna Valdez, and decides within months to become a collaboratore di giustizia. He will eventually take responsibility for cutting off Aldo Semerari's head, in an interview given long afterward, and the judges will not believe him: the men he names as executants are acquitted. Asked about him after the Peru arrest, she gives the sentence that closes twenty-three years. No source found supplies the date of the remark, only the occasion.
stops.quote: Per me Umberto non esiste più; resta solo il padre dei miei figli, che gli vogliono bene e lo rispettano come è loro dovere
stops.quote_source: Statement to the press after Umberto Ammaturo's arrest in Peru; quoted in it.wikipedia, 'Assunta Maresca'
suggested_refs: Ammaturo's collaboration statements, 1993 onward, unexamined

stops.name: Rome, the court orders the film uncut
stops.date_confidence: attested by it.wikipedia 'Assunta Maresca', citing la Repubblica of 29 June 1994 for the ruling of the Tribunale civile di Roma; the broadcast date within 1994 is not given by the Italian source, nor is the channel. The Rai Tre detail comes from English Wikipedia alone. Coordinates are the centre of Rome, supplied by the atlas; the court is not a canonical atlas pin.
stops.campa: The civil tribunal of Rome rules that Il caso Pupetta Maresca may be broadcast without cuts or censorship, because it does not injure the reputation of its subject. It airs complete that year, twelve years after she stopped it. The 1994 broadcast is not a delay that ran out; it is a judgment against her, and the ground of the judgment is that a court examined her reputation and found nothing in the film capable of damaging it further. She is fifty-nine, and the ruling is delivered in a city she has no other business in.
suggested_refs: The 1994 ruling of the Tribunale civile di Roma on Il caso Pupetta Maresca

stops.name: Naples, the apartment becomes an office
stops.date_confidence: attested by it.wikipedia 'Assunta Maresca', citing la Repubblica of 26 February 2004 under the headline 'Casa di Pupetta Maresca diventa sede di volontariato'. English Wikipedia carries the fact without the source, and an earlier pass in this research mis-attributed it to the English article. Canonical Naples pin; the address is not documented.
stops.campa: The Comune di Napoli converts her former apartment into an office for social services and volunteer work. la Repubblica runs it in February 2004 under a headline about the house of Pupetta Maresca becoming a seat of volunteering. The rooms where the diva of crime lived are now a desk where the city hands out assistance. She is sixty-nine and living on the other side of the bay, or in Sorrento, depending on which encyclopedia is asked. The article naming the address of the flat has not been found.
suggested_refs: Comune di Napoli property and social-services records for the 2004 conversion

stops.name: Sorrento, the retirement the sources cannot agree on
stops.date_confidence: CONTRADICTION, unresolved. it.wikipedia: 'Chiusi i negozi di Napoli, si ritiro a Castellammare di Stabia.' English Wikipedia has her living alone in Sorrento. No source has her dividing her time between the two, and the synthesis drafted in an earlier pass of this research is withdrawn as unsupported. 2005 is a placeholder for the retirement years and is not attested. Coordinates are Piazza Tasso, Sorrento.
stops.campa: The Italian record says she closed the Naples shops and withdrew to Castellammare di Stabia, the town she was born in. The English record says she lived alone in Sorrento. Both cannot be a full account and neither can be discarded; an earlier pass of this research settled the conflict by having her divide her time between them, which no source says. Sorrento stands here and Castellammare at her death, with the years between the two left open where the sources leave them.
suggested_refs: Residence registrations for Assunta Maresca after 1986, unexamined

stops.name: Castellammare di Stabia, Arcuri on television
stops.date_confidence: attested; the miniseries is dated 2013 by it.wikipedia and English Wikipedia, and the statement to the press to 7 June 2013 by interris.it, the day after the first episode aired. Pin inherited byte-identically from pasquale_simonetti_pascalone_e_nola.journey.json.
stops.campa: Canale 5 broadcasts Pupetta, il coraggio e la passione, directed by Luciano Odorisio with Manuela Arcuri in the title part. Anti-Camorra campaigners object that it glamorizes the thing it dramatizes. The day after the first episode, at seventy-eight, she answers in her own words for the last widely reported time, and the answer is the one she gave in the dock in 1959. Arcuri is the fourth screen version of her after Schiaffino, herself, and Mussolini, and this time no court is asked to stop anything.
stops.quote: Ho pagato con lacrime e affanno le mie scelte. La prima volta perché l'uomo a cui ho sparato avrebbe fatto lo stesso con me. Cosa dovevo fare, farmi uccidere? Ero incinta.
stops.quote_source: Statement to the press, 7 June 2013, the day after the first episode of the Canale 5 series aired; quoted in interris.it
suggested_refs: Pupetta, il coraggio e la passione (2013), dir. Luciano Odorisio, Canale 5

stops.name: Castellammare di Stabia, she dies at eighty-six
stops.date_confidence: attested by ANSA, Fanpage, English Wikipedia, it.wikipedia, theweek.in and a WION obituary. Pin inherited byte-identically at 40.6952, 14.483; the values 40.6978 and 40.6989 drafted in this pass are not used. Her burial place is named by nothing consulted and is recorded as a gap.
stops.campa: She dies in the town she was born in, in the last days of the year, sixty-six years and five months after her husband was shot on Corso Novara. She was the first woman the Italian press called a camorrista. She outlived Cutolo, the Nuova Famiglia, and the exchange at Corso Novara. No source consulted names her burial place, not the cemetery, not the plot, not the stone. Her every court appearance was photographed; the cemetery registers for January 2022 are unexamined.
suggested_refs: Cemetery registers of Castellammare di Stabia, January 2022, unexamined

stops.name: Castellammare di Stabia, the funeral forbidden
stops.date_confidence: CONTRADICTION on the date, unresolved. Il Fatto Quotidiano of 1 January 2022 places the private blessing of the coffin on 31 December 2021; pasquale_simonetti_pascalone_e_nola.journey.json records ANSA, Fanpage and Il Fatto Quotidiano as reporting the ban on 1 January 2022, the morning the rite had been scheduled. Both readings are printed. The lawyers' objection is single-sourced and stands as reconstruction.
stops.campa: The Questore and the Prefect forbid a public funeral. A service had been arranged at Sant'Antonio di Padova; it does not take place, and about ten women gather at the church to pray instead. Only a private blessing of the coffin is allowed, at the cemetery. Her lawyers object that the word camorrista in the official justification is defamatory, since no court convicted her of it. Her husband's funeral went unrecorded by anyone. Hers is on the record because the state refused to allow it.
suggested_refs: The Questura di Napoli order prohibiting the funeral, December 2021

stops.name: Naples, the letter to the police
stops.date_confidence: attested; the quotation is verbatim from The Guardian of 31 December 2021 and is independently corroborated by Alexander Lucie-Smith's Substack. An earlier pass of this research attributed it to Christina Newland's Substack, which was fetched in full and does not contain it. Canonical Naples pin; the letter's place of writing is not documented.
stops.campa: Francesco Emilio Borrelli, a regional councillor for Europa Verde, writes to the Naples police about what is appearing on social media in the days after her death. The Guardian prints the letter. The letter asks for no charge and names no offence; it objects to what people are posting. Its full text has not been published, and no response from the Questura is recorded in any source consulted. The headline over it calls her a mafia boss, which no Italian court ever found her to be.
stops.quote: We are seeing on social media a glorification of this woman who is a symbol of the Camorra in our neighbourhood. The mythologising of bosses is to be avoided at all costs.
stops.quote_source: Francesco Emilio Borrelli, letter to the Naples police, quoted in The Guardian, 'She understood her power: the death of mafia boss Pupetta Maresca', 31 December 2021
suggested_refs: Borrelli's letter to the Questura di Napoli, December 2021, text unpublished in full

stops.name: Rome, the books after the fact
stops.date_confidence: CONTRADICTION on the day: booksellers' listings give 21 April 2023, Amazon gives 15 April, and an earlier pass of this research recorded 24 April. Gremese Editore, 176 pages, series 'Narratori francesi contemporanei', translated by Franco Ferrini: this is the Italian edition, not a French first edition. Marmo's article is 'La rima amore/onore di Pupetta Maresca. Una primadonna nella camorra degli anni cinquanta', Meridiana 67 (Viella, Rome, 2010), pp. 113-143, JSTOR 23204928. Coordinates are the centre of Rome, the publisher's city.
stops.campa: Philippe Vilain's novel Pupetta appears from Gremese in Italian, tracing her from adolescence to the pardon of 1965. Barbie Latza Nadeau's The Godmother had come out the year before. Marcella Marmo had already given the 1959 trial its scholarly reading in Meridiana in 2010, under a title that sets the two words the case turned on into rhyme: amore and onore. Clare Longrigg reached English readers with her in 1998. Of these, none has been read in full here; each is known by citation only.
suggested_refs: Marcella Marmo, Meridiana 67 (2010), pp. 113-143, JSTOR 23204928
Barbie Latza Nadeau, The Godmother (2022)
Clare Longrigg, Mafia Women (1998)
